title: Act I, Scene III
focus: Juliet, her mother and the Nurse

teacherSummary.text: Lady Capulet calls Juliet to discuss marriage; the Nurse interrupts with a long, bawdy story of Juliet's weaning and her late husband's joke. Lady Capulet describes Paris as a fine book that needs only a cover and asks if Juliet can love him. Juliet agrees to look at him, but no more than her mother allows.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Act I, Scene III (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of Juliet, her mother and the Nurse. writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Act I, Scene III suggests about Juliet, her mother and the Nurse. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the scene's characterization and diction / vocabulary), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how William Shakespeare uses characterization in Act I, Scene III to complicate the reader's understanding of Juliet, her mother and the Nurse. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Act I, Scene III within its historical and literary context and argue how the scene's treatment of Juliet, her mother and the Nurse responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Act I, Scene III alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the scene's handling of Juliet, her mother and the Nurse follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Act I, Scene III and its treatment of Juliet, her mother and the Nurse. State your method, show what it reveals in the scene's characterization and diction / vocabulary, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Act I, Scene III as evidence for a larger claim about Juliet, her mother and the Nurse in Romeo and Juliet. Connect close reading of the scene to the whole play, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Act I, Scene III as a hinge in the play's larger treatment of Juliet, her mother and the Nurse. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Romeo and Juliet.

symbolsAndMotifs.name: light and dark
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: The lovers describe each other as light in darkness (torches, sun, stars, lightning), yet they can meet only at night, and daylight brings danger. In this scene: “odd, of all days in the year, / Come Lammas-eve at night shall she be fourteen. / Susan and she—God rest all Christian souls” (Act I, Scene III, Nurse (speech 11)).

symbolsAndMotifs.name: haste and time
symbolsAndMotifs.explanation: Everything happens too fast: a four-day action, a marriage the day after meeting, a wedding moved up a day; Friar Laurence warns "they stumble that run fast." In this scene: “Faith, I can tell her age unto an hour” (Act I, Scene III, Nurse (speech 7)).

followUps: What in the text makes you think so?
Does anyone read that line differently? What would change?
items.answerGuidance: A defensible line of argument: Juliet enters as a dutiful daughter who promises nothing beyond what her mother allows. Useful evidence: “She’s not fourteen” (Act I, Scene III, Lady Capulet (speech 8)): The Nurse establishes Juliet's age. On setting: The Nurse's earthquake memory places Juliet's childhood in a world of household intimacy. Credit any position that is supported by quotation and reasoning; push one-sided answers to address the strongest counterpoint.

middleSchool.note: Excerpt-based: read the passage aloud first; use the scaffolds; accept partial answers and build with probes.

hsFreshman.note: Use the scaffolds for literal and inferential items; require one quotation for every inferential answer.

hsSophomore.note: Require a quotation and an explanation; push evaluative answers to address a counterclaim.

hsJunior.note: Emphasize structure and ambiguity; students should name where the text leaves matters open.

hsSenior.note: Weigh competing interpretations; students should defend the stronger reading.

ap.note: Treat each evaluative item as a thesis rehearsal: defensible claim, purposeful evidence, commentary on choices.

collegeFreshman.note: Add the extension: connect answers to historical context and one secondary perspective.

collegeSophomore.note: Use the extensions: genre and period conventions, and a published critic.

collegeJunior.note: Use the extensions: name a critical method and test it against the passage.

collegeSenior.note: Use the extensions: connect the scene to the whole work and the scholarship.

graduate.note: Use the extensions: position answers in a critical conversation and the textual history.
